items.headline: Nvidia reinstates Huang; Congress plans hearings
items.summary: Nvidia restored Jensen Huang as chief executive two weeks after he resigned, and President Trump said he pushed for the move. Lawmakers reacted angrily and are moving ahead with hearings over the administration's role and national security concerns.

items.headline: Court opens path for Trump to fight hush money verdict
items.summary: A federal appeals court ruled that Trump's hush money case can be considered for removal to federal court, where he could seek dismissal on presidential immunity grounds. A lower federal court must now decide whether the case moves.

items.headline: Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after ethics report
items.summary: California Democrat Jimmy Gomez said he will resign after the House Ethics Committee found substantial evidence he made unwelcome sexual advances toward a staffer. The committee said his conduct violated House rules.

items.headline: Trump pauses Iowa lead azide detonation pending court
items.summary: President Trump said the Army will not detonate degraded lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant without approval from a federal appeals court. Residents and lawmakers had raised concerns that the blast could spread lead dust widely.

items.headline: Russia warns Estonia of 'open war' over border
items.summary: Russia accused Estonia of hostilities it said are on the verge of triggering open war, escalating tensions on NATO's eastern flank. Estonia plans to close its border crossings with Russia.

items.headline: Storms add to Thanksgiving travel worries
items.summary: Storms forecast for both coasts this week are threatening Thanksgiving travel after a string of airline technology failures. Airlines have largely recovered from the glitches, but travelers remain uneasy.

items.headline: Colorado judge holds ICE in contempt
items.summary: A federal judge in Colorado held Immigration and Customs Enforcement in contempt for ignoring orders barring the immediate re-arrest of detainees a court had ordered released. Judges there say the agency has repeatedly re-arrested the same people.

items.headline: Democrats probe Trump Jr.-linked businesses
items.summary: House Democrats are investigating whether companies tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s investment firm, 1789 Capital, have benefited from government access. Investigators say the companies have profited since his father's reelection.

items.headline: South Korea's education minister resigns
items.summary: South Korea's education minister stepped down after backlash over measures to stop AI-assisted cheating on the national college entrance exam. The resignation follows criticism of how the anti-AI rules were handled.

items.headline: Congo residents sue Chinese-owned mine over pollution
items.summary: Twenty-seven residents of the Democratic Republic of Congo are suing a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine, alleging its pollution poisoned their community. They also accuse the government of failing to protect them.

digest.overview:
Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, and President Trump said "I convinced them." Sen. Chuck Schumer promised a Democratic investigation, and Huang faces House committee interviews Dec. 1. A federal appeals court opened a path for Trump to move his hush money case to federal court. Rep. Jimmy Gomez of California said he will resign after an ethics report found he made unwelcome advances toward a staffer. Trump said the Army will not blow up degraded explosives in Iowa without a court's approval. A federal judge in Colorado held ICE in contempt over repeated re-arrests of released detainees. Pennsylvania reported its ninth measles death of the year as its outbreak passed 1,600 cases. Storms threaten Thanksgiving travel on both coasts.

Abroad, Russia summoned Estonia's envoy and said Tallinn's plan to close all border crossings from Dec. 1 is "on the verge of triggering open war." Russia launched 96 drones at Ukraine overnight, and Libya's Tripoli government demanded answers from Kyiv over its drone strike on Russian ships. The European Commission proposed a 22nd sanctions package cutting 60 more Russian banks from SWIFT. Iran vowed to use "all available means" against the U.S. naval blockade as Vice President Vance and Secretary Rubio met Qatar's prime minister. South Korea scrambled fighter jets after Russian military aircraft entered its air defense zone near Ulleungdo, and North Korea threatened to close Switzerland's new office in Pyongyang. The WHO chief called for peace in Congo's Ebola-hit Ituri province.

fact.answer:
Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water. As water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock its molecules into an open, hexagonal crystal lattice that holds them farther apart than in the liquid, making ice about 9 percent less dense. That is why roughly a tenth of an ice cube or iceberg sits above the surface.

Most substances get denser as they cool, but water is densest at about 4°C (39°F). In a lake, chilled surface water sinks until the whole lake nears that temperature, so ice forms on top rather than the bottom. Air trapped in ice changes only slightly how high it floats.

The takeaway: floating ice lets life survive beneath frozen lakes, and the same expansion is why a soda can can burst in the freezer.
fact.question: Why does ice float on water?
